_note: Curator decisions for the 2026-11-17 pilot release. Every staged claim has an explicit category and reason. Only proposed_include rows carry patient-facing text. Nothing here is approval: owner decisions are recorded separately as owner_reviewed_for_pilot.
id_reservation: CLM-701..CLM-799 are reserved for curator-authored release claims (the daily-discovery allocator continues from CLM-253 and would never collide in practice; tests assert no overlap).

authored_claims.normalizedClaim: In a small randomized, open-label trial of 56 people with ulcerative colitis in remission who had iron-deficiency anaemia, daily and alternate-day oral iron did not differ significantly in haemoglobin, red-cell indices or iron measures after 8 weeks, nor in side effects or disease flares.
authored_claims.exactSupportingExcerpt: Our study did not show any significant difference in mean hemoglobin levels, RBC indices, or iron profiles between the daily and alternate-day oral iron groups.
authored_claims.studyPopulation: Adults with ulcerative colitis in remission and iron-deficiency anaemia (n = 56)
authored_claims.studyDesign: Randomized, open-label trial; daily vs alternate-day oral iron; primary outcome mean change in haemoglobin at 8 weeks
authored_claims.limitations: 56 participants, open-label, 8 weeks, one oral iron formulation, single country; the authors say larger studies are needed. 'No significant difference' does not prove the two schedules are equivalent.

authored_claims.normalizedClaim: A German guideline update on ulcerative colitis surgery (status November 2025) states that in acute severe ulcerative colitis, colectomy (surgery to remove the colon) is still indicated when standard drug treatment has failed; in selected cases a JAK inhibitor can be considered as an alternative third-line treatment in specialised centres.
authored_claims.exactSupportingExcerpt: In patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis, colectomy is still indicated for treatment after failure of standard pharmacotherapy, in selected cases a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor can be considered as an alternative third line treatment in centers.
authored_claims.exactLocator: PubMed abstract (PMID 43026331), first sentence; Chirurgie 2026 (German-language guideline summary with English abstract)
authored_claims.studyPopulation: Adults with acute severe ulcerative colitis who failed standard pharmacotherapy
authored_claims.studyDesign: National clinical practice guideline (surgery chapter), abstract-level summary
authored_claims.evidenceStrength: national guideline statement (abstract only; strength-of-recommendation grading not stated in the abstract)
authored_claims.limitations: German national guideline summarised in a journal abstract; the recommendation grade, evidence level and the full text were not read. Applicability to Canada/US care pathways is not assessed. Decisions about surgery are made with the treating team.

CLM-115.patient: If you have ulcerative colitis and feel well (symptomatic remission), the AGA guideline suggests checking a biomarker test together with your symptoms, rather than relying on symptoms alone.
CLM-115.reason: UC-specific AGA practice guideline recommendation; excerpt is verbatim and the claim restates it without adding.

CLM-116.patient: If you have ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, the AGA guideline suggests that a fecal calprotectin below 150 µg/g, a normal fecal lactoferrin and/or a normal CRP can be used to rule out active inflammation, so routine endoscopy can be avoided.
CLM-116.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; thresholds are decision thresholds, not individual diagnoses (stated in limitations).

CLM-117.patient: If you have ulcerative colitis with moderate-to-severe symptoms, the AGA guideline suggests that a fecal calprotectin above 150 µg/g, an elevated fecal lactoferrin or an elevated CRP can help guide treatment decisions without routine endoscopy.
CLM-117.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; verbatim excerpt.

CLM-118.patient: When symptoms and biomarker tests disagree (feeling well but raised markers, or moderate-to-severe symptoms with normal markers), the AGA guideline suggests an endoscopic assessment to guide treatment.
CLM-118.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation addressing a common patient question (do symptoms always match inflammation?).

CLM-119.patient: If you have ulcerative colitis with only mild symptoms, the AGA guideline suggests an endoscopic assessment of disease activity to guide treatment decisions.
CLM-119.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; verbatim excerpt.

CLM-120.patient: The AGA guideline panel noted it is not yet known whether monitoring with biomarkers is better than monitoring with endoscopy; it listed this as a knowledge gap.
CLM-120.reason: UC-specific guideline statement of uncertainty; included so the agent can say what is NOT known rather than overstate biomarkers.

CLM-121.patient: The AGA guideline concludes that non-invasive tests, including fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin and blood CRP, can inform monitoring and management of ulcerative colitis.
CLM-121.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline conclusion; verbatim excerpt.

CLM-126.patient: The STRIDE-II consensus says histological healing in ulcerative colitis is not a formal treatment target but should be assessed as a measure of how deep remission is.
CLM-126.reason: IBD-general consensus with an explicit ulcerative-colitis statement; the claim keeps the source's 'not a formal target' wording. If approved its claim-level applicability is recorded as ulcerative_colitis (the source stays IBD-general) so the app can serve it.
CLM-126.strength: expert consensus recommendation (systematic review + Delphi, 89 IOIBD members; 13 of 15 recommendations endorsed)

CLM-701.reason: Human randomized trial in UC; excerpt is a direct, appropriately hedged result. Small open-label trial: strength recorded as low.

CLM-702.reason: UC-specific national guideline statement on acute severe UC and colectomy; fills a surgery/urgent-care coverage gap. Abstract-level only.
